title: English spelling froze just as its vowels went on the move
body: Between roughly 1400 and 1700, the long vowels of English shifted in a chain, each moving to a new position in the mouth. Meanwhile, spelling was starting to settle into fixed forms. The result is a writing system that often records late medieval pronunciation: the letters in ‘bite’, ‘meet’ and ‘name’ once matched their sounds far better than they do today.

slides.prompt: Around 1400, what did the English word ‘mouse’ sound like?
slides.detail: And ‘bite’ sounded roughly like ‘beet’. Between about 1400 and 1700 the long vowels shifted in a chain, while the spelling stayed put.

slides.heading: Before the shift
slides.text: Around 1400, ‘bite’ sounded roughly like today’s ‘beet’, ‘meet’ like a drawn-out ‘met’, and ‘mouse’ much like ‘moose’.

slides.heading: A chain reaction
slides.text: The highest vowels became diphthongs: the ‘ee’ of ‘bite’ turned into ‘eye’ and the ‘oo’ of ‘mouse’ into ‘ow’. Other vowels moved up to fill the gaps.

steps.label: The highest vowels break into diphthongs
Lower vowels move up to fill the gaps
Spelling settles, so the letters stay put

slides.heading: German respelled
slides.text: German went through a similar change but updated its spelling, so medieval ‘mūs’ became ‘Maus’. English kept its old letters, and they drifted out of step.

slides.heading: The North held out
slides.text: In Scots and older northern speech, the long ‘oo’ of ‘house’ never shifted, which is why Scots still says ‘hoose’ and ‘oot’.

slides.heading: How did it sound around 1400?
slides.explanation: Before the shift the letters matched the sounds far better: ‘bite’ was ‘beet’, ‘mouse’ was ‘moose’ and ‘meet’ a long ‘met’.
